The House met at eleven of the clock, Mr. Chairman in the chair, 
THE FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF INDIA'S VICTORY IN KARGIL 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon Members, July 26,2000 marks the first anniversary of 
india's victory in the Kargil conflict when the last of the Pakistani aggressors were 
evicted from our territory. Recalling the sacrifices of many of our brave  soldiers and 
airmen who laid down their lives to protect the territorial integrity of India and the acts 
of courage and gallantry displayed by our troops, this  House saltues the memory of 
those who were k illed in defending the motherland ant. applauds the dedication and 
professional commitment of the members of  our armed forces. This House reaffirms 
the nation's commitment to the welfare of the families of the martyrs and of those who 
were disabled. This House also  recalls, with pride and joy, the great unity, solidarity 
and sense of purpose that  the entire nation displayed during the crisis which 
demonstrated India's unshakeable resolve to foil any misadventure of the kind that our 
neighbour regrettably engaged herself in. 
Today, on the occasion of the Kargil Vijay Diwas, this House reiterates India's 
resolve to beat back any aggression as well as our commitment to the path of peace 
and maintenance of good relations with our neighbours.

Kutir Jyoti Programme for Rural Areas 
†*41. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL:†† 
          DR. D. MASTHAN; 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a programme namely Kutir Jyoti Programme was launched 
to provide electricity in the houses of families living below poverty line in the country, 
particularly in rural and tribal areas; 
(b) if so, the percentage of poor families in rural areas who have been provided with 
electricity under Kutir Jyoti Programme till December 1999; and 
(c) by when the remaining families are likely to be provided with electricity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMAT1 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Government of India launched Kutir Jyoti Programme in 1988-89 
for extending single point light connection to the households of rural families below 
poverty line including Harijan and Adivasi families. More than

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.R. KUMARAMANGALAM): Sir, with your 
permission, I would like to answer. I think the hon. Member if I may submit, I should 
really apologise to him is justified in saying that he had put a very straight question. We 
are revealing the answer. The truth of the matter if that the figure is not very 
complimentary. The total figure is 487.92 lakhs BPL households throughout the country. 
Out of that, we have done only 35 lakhs through our scheme. Though the amount 
involved is Rs. 214.6 crores, the misfortune, perhaps, is that most of these single-light 
connections are connections where meters are not really fixed. In the name of single-
light connection, in many of the cases, more power than a single-light connection is 
actually drawn. The Electricity Boards are relu ctant to use this grant. This is purely a 
grant. They are reluctant to use this grant. We have been pressurising them. In fact, in 
my own home State, I had to pressurise the Electricity Board Chairman to take a little 
more and we are still trying with each other to increase the figure. It is something where we 
need the help of Members of Parliament to make them understand that unless we get our 
households connected with power, there is no use of talking about full electrification. I 
agree with the hon. Member that this is a matter which needs real attention. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: But, at least, the exact figures should be given to us. They 
should be given to me in writing. 
SHRI P.R. KUMARAMANGALAM: I will give you the figures.

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2000] 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: Sir, the major problem, as stated by Shri Kapil 
Sibal, is it has come down to 3000 in the Ninth Plan. It is not a question of forcing the 
State Electricity Boards. It is because of the new power policy which you have framed. 
The Boards feel that this is absolutely unremunerative. It is unremunerative in the sense 
that you are giving a grant. Up to giving a grant, it is all right. The remuneration is Rs. 
5/- per connection which is becoming totally unremunerative for the Boards. The State 
Government as well as the Central Government  have to decide about the subsidy. This 
has nothing to do with the Boards. Whatever is the target; let us quantify it financially. 
Subsidy is required for the people who cannot pay more than Rs. 5/-. Even tribal areas 
are involved in it. That is why it is not remunerative. Even 50 per cent of the generation 
cost cannot be collected from them. So far as these targeted sections of BPL and tribals 
are concerned, the only decision which we have to take here is, beyond Rs. 5/- 
whatever is the subsidy, let it be shared byboth the State Government and the Central 
Government. If you leave it to the Boards, it will never be possible. You can go on 
forcing them. Can we not decide here as to what is the financial quantification? If you 
really mean business, so far as the BPL people and tribals are concerned, this subsidy 
beyond Rs. 5/- has to be shared by the Central Government and the State Government 
as a poverty alleviation programme, not as a State Electricity Board programme. 
SHRI P.R. KUMARAMANGALAM; Sir, I do agree with the hon. Member. The real 
issue which the Boards are facing is, after giving the connections, as I said earlier, there 
is no income from these connections. Often, a single light  connection becomes not a 
single light connection. Therefore, it is more than calculated system. This is the issue 
which is arising. This is a very genuine issue. In a country which is a developing 
country, there has to be some transparent subsidy available for the weaker sections of 
the society. Now, in certain States, they have prioritised it differently. For example, in 
my State, it is for agriculture and also, by the way, for single light connection. In some 
States, they don't do it. Insofar as Centre's contribution is concerned, we are actually 
giving subsidy by indirect methods. But I think it is much better to look at these things 
transparently. The suggestion of the hon. Member would be looked at very seriously. 
We have a group of Ministers within the Ministry of Rural Electrification, because even 
in rural electrification, getting wire from an urban area or, may be from the main grid into 
a village is uneconomic. Even in UP, it costs Rs. 5-6 lakhs a village; and that village 
does not generate the

†*42.   SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN:†† 
             SHRI V.V.RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to stale: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item as appeared 
in 'The Hindustan Times' dated the 8th June, 2000, under the caption "Christian School 
Principal murdered near Mathura"; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) how many such incidents on attack on Christian minority run institutions have 
taken place in Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Orissa during the year 2000 so far and 
Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI I. 
D. SWAMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) As per available information, from the Government of Uttar Pradesh, Brother 
George, a warden of St. Francis School (earlier known as Brother Pauls's Memorial 
School) Hostel at Navada under Narhouli Police Station, Mathura was attacked and 
killed by 6-7 assailants on the night of 6th-7th June, 2000, while he was asleep in the 
hostel compound. A case under Section 396 of the IPC was registered at the Narhouli 
Police Station. The matter was handed over to the Crime Branch of the State Police and 
a judicial Inquiry has also been ordered by the State Government under a one-man 
Commission headed by a sitting Judge of the Allahabad High Court. 
(c) As per available information, six incidents have been reported on minority run 
institutions in Uttar Pradesh during this year. No such incidents have been reported in 
this regard from the States of Gujarat and Orissa. 
Besides sharing intelligence inputs, sending advisories from time to time, another 
advisory has been sent to all States/UTs on 19-6-2000, and a high-level meeting, 
consisting of Home Secretaries, DGPs/IGs of Andhra Pradesh, U.P., Karnataka, Goa, 
Orissa and Gujarat, was convened on 4-7-2000 to review the situation, and the State 
Government have been asked to provide security to the minorities and their institutions 
and to deal firmly with the perpetrators of violence against them.

Discussions on security issues with Israel 
399. SHRI C. M. IBRAHIM: W ill the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether during his recent visit to Israel, he discussed security aspects, 
especially the need to counter terrorism as a global menace and counter intelligence 
measures;

(c) how it has affected India's relation with Middle-East, Arab and Gulf countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI CH. 
VIDYASAGAR RAO): (a) to (c) During the recent visit to Israel, we 
interacted with President Ezer Weizman, Prime Minister Ehud Barak, Minister for 
Regional Co-operation Shimon Peres, Deputy Minister of Defence Ephriam Sneh, and 
Police and Security agencies. The tour was undertaken with the main focus on problems of 
trans-border terrorism. Israel and India have both grappled with it during the last two 
decades. Terrorist organisations are now known to establish and have international 
linkages which makes it necessary for victim countries to learn from the experience of 
and work in close co-operation with each other in the interest of promotion of peace and 
progress and suppression of terrorism. 
The visit has opened up the possibility of increased technological, technical and 
intelligence co-operation between India and Israel. The two sides have agreed to work 
for early establishment of a Joint Working Group between the two countries. 
The visit, which is a part of the ongoing high-level exchanges between the two 
countries, has had no effect on India's traditional ties of friendship and cooperation with the 
Arab countries. Our relations with the Arab world continue to remain substantive, 
multifaceted and wide ranging.

power mainly due to weather beating loads resulting in low voltage in Delhi system. 
Under such critical conditions of low voltage and low frequency, DVB has to resort to 
unscheduled load shedding for the security of its own system and the Northern Grid as a 
whole. En order to mitigate the shortages during summer of 2000, an Action Plan was 
drawn up in November, 1999 for meeting power demand in NCT Delhi. The Action 
Plan envisaged steps for preventive maintenance of generating units, allocation of 
adequate supply of Naphtha and HSD for gas power plants sourcing power supply to 
Delhi, enhancement of allocation to Delhi from 15% unallocated quota to 25%, supply 
of power by HPSEB under bilateral arrangement, strengthening of transmission and 
distribution system in Delhi, preventive  maintenance of tran smission lines/sub-
stations, installation of shunt capacitors etc. and also maximising generation from 
centra! power stations located in the Northern Region etc. The implementation of the 
Action Plan was discussed in December, 1999 and reviewed in May, 2000 in the 
Ministry of Power with all concerned including Delhi Vidyut Board and Government 
of NCT of Delhi. 
(d) Does not arise, in view of (b) and (c) above.

427. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister of

129

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) The Government is in receipt of the Confederation of 
Indian Industries (CII) report on Independent Power Producers (IPPs). 
(b) and (c) The reasons for adequate domestic or foreign investment not fructifying 
in the power sector is not lack of a clear and transparent policy, but various other factors, 
primary among which is the poor financial health of most of the State Electricity Boards 
who do not have the fi nancial capability to s upport more than a few projects in terms of 
regular payment of bills of electricity purchased by them from IPPs. The poor financial 
health of the State Electricity Boards and the insistence by lenders on strong payment 
security packages has been the main problem in the private power projects achieving 
financial closure. With a view to findi ng a solution to this problem and to 
simplify/decentralise the procedure for clearance of private power projects and to 
attract more investment in the power sect or, the Government ha s already initiated 
several measures which include:—  
—  minimising the number of clearances required to be obtained for the purpose 
of appraisal of the private power projects by Central Electricity Authority 
(CEA). 
—  minimising the role of the Foreign Investment Promotion Board by providing 
for automatic approval for foreign equity in selected categories and 
enlarging the provisions for automatic approval for such projects and 
liberalisation of the Foreign Direct Investment regime by removal of the upper 
limit for foreign direct investment in respect of projects relating to electric 
generation, transmission and distributi on (other than atomic reactor power 
plants). 
—  delegating more powers for environmental clearance to State Governments. 
—  raising the financial limits for power projects which require the clearance 
from CEA. 
—  preparation of a shelf of projects to facilitate early execution and reduction 
of time required for implementation. 
—  close monitoring at various levels to expedite clearances, remove bottlenecks 
and to resolve the 'last mile' problems in achieving financial closure.

—  The Electricity Laws Amendment, Act, 1998 was enacted to make

—  A policy on Hydro Power Development has been initiated for accelerating

electric potential at faster pace, incr ease the private investment and promote

430. SHRI R.P. GOENKA; Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) The losses being incurred by various State 
Governments on account of power theft are. not being separately assessed. However, 
the experience of States undergoing reforms indicate that the losses on account of T & 
D, theft and pilferage are to the extent of 45% of the power generated. A rough 
estimate indicate that out of the total energy generated only 55% is billed (Rs. 62,000 
crores). Of the amount not billed 20% loss is sustained due to theft and pilferate (Rs. 
22,500 crores). 
A statement showing the percentage T & D losses including both the technical and 
commercial losses as assessed by the concerned State Electricity Boards/Electricity 
Departments for the Year 1997-98 is annexed (See below) 
Quantum jump in the T & D losses reported by the reforming states is apparently 
on the account of the ability of the vertica lly integrated SEBs to misclassify losses. 
This would not be possible in restructur ed generation, transmission and distribution 
utilities. Restructured distribution entities would be under compulsion to assess the 
losses nearer to actuals. 
(c) and (d) Though the power distribu tion falls within the purview of the  State 
Governments and the activities pertaining to prevention of theft of electricity and 
removing illegal connection have  to be taken care of by the power utilities operating 
under their jurisdiction. Theft of electricity has been made a cognizable offence under 
the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, and the utilities have to  effectively implement the 
provisions of the law to curb the theft of electricity. 
In the Common Minimum National Action Plan for power announced in

period of 2 years. 
3. All electric supplies should be metered by 2002 AD.  
4. Compulsory annual energy audit to be ensured in respect of large consumers of 
more than 100 KVA load. 
5. Time of the day metering would be introduced for big power consumers for better 
load management.

T & D losses by energy audit, 100% metering, reduction of power theft and

(c) the quantum of power to be made available at the rate of cost of production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes Sir; in terms of the approved formula for sharing of power 
from Central Sector Hydel Stations, 12% power is to be supplied free of cost to those 
States of the Region (including the State where the hydroelectric project is located) 
where distress by way of submergence/dislocation of population is caused by setting up 
the project. The Allocation to the State in which the project is located where the entire 
distress takes place is 12 percent. If the distress affects more than one State then the 
allocation is made in proportion to the extent of distress. 
(b) The project authorities, na mely, Nathpa Jhakri Power Corporation (NJPC) has 
estimated that the annual revenue available to Himachal Pradesh by the sale of free 
power would be about Rs. 2.04.57 crores based on the tariff of Rs. 2.57 per unit for the 
first year of operation. 
(c) In terms of provisions contained in Articles of Association of NJPC, after supply 
of 12% power free of cost to Himachal Pradesh, the balance (88%) of power from 
Nathpa Jhakri H.E. Project (1500 MW) would be distributed at bus bar rates as under:— 
(i)25% of the remaining &8% of gene rated power shall be allocated to 
Government of Himachal Pradesh in lieu of 25% cost sharing of the project by 
Government of Himachal Pradesh. 
(ii) the remaining 66% of generated power shall be at the disposal of the 
Government of India in lieu of 75% of cost sharing of the project by the 
Government of India and shall be allocated by the Government of India to 
various States of the region (including Himachal Pradesh) in accordance with 
the approved formula.

DEVELOPMENT (SHRI SUBHASH MAHARIA): (a) to (c) Jawahar Rozgar Yojana 
(JRY) was introduced w.e.f. 1.4.1989. The scheme was implemented throughout the 
country including Arunachal Pradesh except Union Territories of Chandigarh and 
Delhi. The scheme was specifically meant for rural areas and not for towns and cities. 
The objectives of the programme was to provide additional gainful wage employment 
to the rural poor. The programme also aimed at creation of sustained employment by 
strengthening rural economic infrastructure besides creating community and social 
assets for the direct and continuing benefits of the rural poor. Forestry and Horticulture 
were permissible activities under the scheme. The funds under the scheme were utilized 
by the district panchayat, intermediate level panchayat and village panchayat in the 
ratio of 15:15:70 respectively. These institutions were allowed to take up any work as 
per their share of funds and the felt needs of the area. Village-wise details of the works 
undertaken were not monitored at the Central level. 
The erstwhile JRY has been restructured, streamlined and renamed as Jawahar Gram 
Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) w i t h  effect from 1.4.99. The primary objective of the 
programme is to create dema nd driven village infrastr ucture. The programme is 
implemented by the village panchayat with the approval of Gram Sabha. Forestry and 
Horticulture continue to remain permissible activities under the JGSY.

463. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed the implementation of the Technology 
Upgradation Fund Scheme for Textile and Jute industries; 
(b) if so, the details thereof;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) and (b) The Government have 
constituted a 22 members Inter-Ministerial Steering Committee (IMSC), under the 
Chairmanship of Secretary (Textiles), for reviewing and monitoring the implementation 
of the Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) for the textile and jute industries. 
The IMSC has been reviewing and monitoring the implementation of TUFS on a regular 
basis, and has so far held 5 meetings. It is an ongoing exercise. On the basis of feed-back 
received from various quarters, the IMSC has reviewed the scheme and taken a number of 
decisions for effective implementation of the scheme. The important decisions taken are 
as under: 
(i) The loans which were sanctioned prior to 1-4-1999; but not disbursed can be 
considered under TUFS as fresh cases, if otherwise they meet the parameters 
of TUFS. 
(ii) In case a part disbursed loans, if the borrower wishes to be considered for 
TUFS benefits, a fresh project conforming to TUFS norms can be submitted 
to the lending agency after terminating the existing loan cases. 
(iii) In respect of Captive Power Generation, ceiling on investment has 
been relaxed. 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2000] 
(iv) The energy s a v i n g  devices, effluent treatment p l a n ts  and water treatment 
plants can be installed without any ceiling on investment. 
(v) The preliminary and pre-operative expenses and incremental margin money on 
working capital have been included as eligible investment under the scheme. 
(vi) Yarn processing has been made an additional eligible downstream value 
addition activity for investment in capacity expansion in cotton ring spinning 
mills. 
(vii) The maximum expired life (vintage) of certain second hand machinery has 
been enhanced from 5 years to 10 years. 
(viii)Semi-automatic looms are now allowed for decentralised powerloom sector. 
(ix) Air jet looms of 165 cms. width (capable of manufacturing 60 inch width Grey 
fabrics) and similar width in case of Water Jet looms and also automatic 
shuttle looms are eligible under TUFS.

applications with a total project cost of Rs. 7668 crore were received. Out of them,

Rs. 904 crore has been disbursed against 232 applications 
(d) and (e) A number of representations have been received from various quarters 
for relaxation in financial norms of the nodal/co-opted financial agencies. Representations 
have been duly considered, and important decisions taken in this regard are as under:

continuous profit for availing of loan for the units which are viable, having 
good track record with a positive net worth even though they had incurred 
losses.

other cases. IDBI agreed to relax it even upto 17.5% in extremely deserving 
cases.

Residential permits for refugees in Delhi 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa); Madam, India is one of the 
countries in the world with largest number of refugees. At this moment, in 
India, there are about one lakh Tibetans and another one lakh Sri Lankan 
refugees. In addition, there are also about 20,000 refugees in the capital city 
of Delhi, out of which about 15.000 are Afghans and the rest are Burmese. 
Somalis. Sudanese, Iranians and some others. The majority of Afghan 
refugees are Hindus and Sikhs of Indian origin. In addition to refugees from 
foreign countries, we also have a large number of internalry displaced persons 
from Kashmir and the North-Eastern region, who suffer a similar plight. There 
is presently no law in India to deal with the refugee situation. Such a law is 
essential to prevent arbitrariness, ad-hocism and abuse of power at lower 
levels of bureaucratic decision-making. An Eminent Persons Group, 
including former Chief Justice of India, Justice P.N. Bhagwati, submitted last 
year to the Government of India a draft Refugees and Asylum Seekers 
Protection Act, 2000." Our own colleague, the former Chief Justice of India, 
Shri Ranganath Misra, played an important role in this respect when he was 
the Chairman of the Human Rights Commission. As per this Act, persons 
who are guilty of crimes against humanity, drug trafficking, acts of terrorism 
or are members of political groups banned in India, are not entitled to 
refugee status. The Government should bring this legislation before 
Parliament, and in the meanwhile, even if the Government does not want to 
put a legislation as 
190 

[26 JULY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
such, a Manual of Practices and Procedures on refugee matters for the use 
of the administration dealing with the subject,, should be immediately 
prepared and finalized. It is also necessary to provide immediately 
residential permits to all refugees who have been accepted in India, 
particularly in urban areas like Delhi, in the interest of national security and 
in the interest of refugees themselves. Thank you.

SHRI B. P. SINGHAL (Uttar Pradesh): Madam Deputy Chairperson, this 
Bill is an amendment to the parent Act, and that parent Act deals with the 
disposal of the property of those who have been declared as deserters or 
who have died a natural death or, otherwise, who are not there any more. The 
parent Act was enacted to see to it that the entire responsibility of paying all 
the dues that belonged to an Army or an Air Force personnel devolved on 
the Commanding Officer; that duty was devolved on the Commanding 
Officer to collect that amount and then have it paid to the heirs whose names 
were already mentioned in the officer's service record. Now, why is this 
amount sought to be increased? In 1954, when I joined the IPS, my salary 
was Rs.350/-. At that time, a constable's or a jawan's salary used to be so 
low that the total cumulative gratuity, PF, did not, perhaps, come to even Rs. 
10,0007-. Today, the salaries have gone up and, naturally, all-these amounts will 
be much more. So, in keeping with that, the limit has been increased to Rs.2 
lakhs and I hope that this limit wiil be sufficient to take care of most of them. 
Hon. Member, Shri Pachouri, raised a very relevant point about war-widows. 
But, that is a totally different subject. We know from Press reports that the 
Army is already seized of the issue, about the kind of problems that parents 
are experiencing or even the wives are experiencing. I think they are 
evolving some methods to ensure that the money is given to the members of 
the family of the diseased. In the title of the Bill also, the word '2000' needs 
to be added. The hon. Minister is, of course, moving an amendment in this 
regard. The only point here was about the change of names of Acts because, 
technically, the word used is 1913' of the Administrator General's Act; it was 
amended in 1963; therefore, it was changed to 1963. Similarly, the Indian 
Lunacy Act, 1912, was amended to become the Mental Health

this Bill as it is. In the Statement of Objects and Reasons it has been 
mentioned, "any person appearing to such authority to be entitled to such 
property and money, without requiring the production of any probate, letter of 
administration, succession certificate or other such conclusive evidence of 
title." Madam, here comes the problem. There is no doubt that this Bill has 
been brought with a laudable object to avoid expenses and troublesome and 
time-consuming procedure. But the difficulties and problems which are going 
-to be faced have also to be taken into consideration while passing this Bill, 
Under the Army Act, nomination by an Army person is provided. An Army 
person can nominate anybody to receive his assets. Now, nominee need not 
necessarily be a Segal heir. Nominee does not necessarily mean all the 
legal heirs. Only one person can be nominated. , He may be or may not be a 
legal heir. Under the Insurance Act, the position is that the nominee is only a 
legal agent. He has to collect the amount and distribute it to the legal heirs. 
Now, that provision itself has to be taken into consideration. Madam, under 
the Hindu Succession Act, wife, son, daughter and mother are the legal heirs 
of a Hindu. But if a nomination is made in favour of a particular person and

heirs, then what will be the position? As a matter of fact, in our place North

taken any steps to help them who were in dire straits. The parents also said 
that Poongavanam had threatened them with dire consequences if they 
came for help to her."   Madam, this is the situation.

THE COTTON CLOTH (REPEAL) BILL, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES {SHRI KASHIRAM RANA): Madam, I 
beg to move: 
"That the Bill to repeal the Cotton Cloth Act, 1918, as passed by 
Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration . 
Madam, the Cotton Cloth Act was enacted in 1918, with a view to 
encouraging and maintaining the supply of standard cotton cloth 
manufactured in the country, at reasonable rates, to the weaker sections of 
society. This Act, has jurisidction to the whole of India. Under the Act, the 
State Governments are empowered to appoint a Controller for 
implementation of its provisions and also an Advisory Committee to assist 
the Controller. The State Governments are also empowered to fix the price 
of the standard cloth, prescribing the authority for grant of licences for sale 
of standard cloth and rute-making power for giving effect to the provisions of 
the Act. The Controller so appointed, is empowered to make general or 
special orders for manufacture, transport, distribution and sale or purchase 
of cotton cloth.   The Controller is also empowered to fix the 
221 

RAJYA. SABHA [26 JULY, 2000] 
price to be paid to the manufacturer, to declare and define the classes of 
standard cloth, etc. This Act also has provisions for imposing penalties for its 
contravention with imprisonment up to 6 months or with fine or with 
both. 
Over the years, the textile industry has been growing steadily. The 
production of cloth from 1980-81 to 1999-2000 has risen by an estimated 
200 per cent at an average annual growth rate of about 6%. The per capita 
availability of cloth, which was 17.30 sq. mt. during 1980-81, rose to 28.19 
sq. mt. during 1998-99 an increase of about 63 per cent showing an average 
growth of 2.75 per cent. Apart from meeting the ever increasing domestic 
need, the export of cotton textiles alone rose from Rs. 400 crore in 1981-82 
to about Rs. 18,000 crore in 1999-2000. 
It is our endeavour to develop a strong and vibrant textile industry 
that can produce cloth of good quality at reasonable prices, which meets the 
growing needs of the people and also contributes to the economic growth of 
the nation while competing with confidence for an increasing share of the 
global market. For this purpose, the Government has taken several steps. 
The Technology Upgradation Funds Scheme (TUFS), that is in operation 
from 1,4.1999 for modernisation of the Textiles and Jute Industries, and the 
Technology Mission of Cotton Development are some such important 
initiatives. 
The Government of India had enacted the Essential Commodities 
Act in 1955. Cotton and textiles are essential commodities under the 
provisions of this Act. In exercise of the powers conferred upon it by Section 
3 of the Essential Commodities Act, Government of India has issued the 
Textile (Development & Regulation ) Order, 1993, which is comprehensive 
and generally covers all the provisions of Cotton Cloth Act, 1918. While the 
Cotton Cloth Act, 1918 deals with only one category viz. Cotton Cloth, the 
Textile (Development & Regulation ) Order 1993, deals with all types of 
cloth, yarn and other textiles. This order is implemented by the Textile 
Commissioner, who is appointed by the Government of India and has 
jurisdiction over entire India. Due to the fact that, man-made fibre textiles 
were not in vogue in 1918, the scope and focus of the Cotton Cloth Act has 
been extremely narrow. Therefore, in the present scenario, the Act is 
superfluous, redundant and irrelevant and deserves to be repealed.

The Cabinet has approved the proposal for repeal of the Cotton 
Cloth Act. 1918. The Commission of Review of Administrative Laws has 
also recommended the repeal of this Act. 
The Lok Sabha passed the Cotton Cloth (Repeal) Bill, 2000 on 5 th 
May, 2000. I request the House to approve the Cotton Cloth (Repeal) Bill, 
2000 as passed by the Lok Sabha. 
The question was proposed. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: We will pass the Bill. There is no 
problem. I will call Shardaji to make her speech, but before she makes her 
speech, t would like to bring to your notice, Mantriji, that you are repealing a 
redundant Bill. Fine. But the situation in respect of the cotton yarn is not 
very good, as far as the handloom people are concerned. Their condition is 
very bad. Some people in Andhra Pradesh are on the verge of committing 
suicide. Even some place in U.P. and in Maharashtra, where they are using 
cotton, while the cotton prices are crashing, the bunkars are not getting 
enough cotton yarn. While you ask us to repeal it, without discussion, from 
the Chair, I am telling you, on behalf of the entire House, which is 
concerned about these people, that khadi is becoming redundant. So, all 
these things you must take into consideration. We assure you that we wilt 
pass the Bill. Why don't you give us some assurance on that, that you will 
take care of the bunkars in the country?

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
New Uplinking Policy 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Madam, earlier, satellite TV 
channels were not permitted to uplink their programmes from India. 
However, as the hon. Members would recollect, satellite based TV channels 
have started beaming their programmes into India by uplinking their 
channels from hubs abroad since early nineties, as the satellite technology 
has become available. As a result, they have remained outside the Indian 
jurisdiction. In order to bring them back under the purview of the Indian laws, 
the uplinking policy was relaxed for the first time on 9.6.1998 and the Indian 
broadcastsg companies with a minimum of 80% Indian share holding and  
Indian management  control were permitted to 
 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [26 JULY, 2000] 
uplink their channels from India but only through VSNL. This permission was 
restricted to only those Indian companies, which were being released foreign 
exchange for uplinking from abroad. The policy was further liberalised on 
26.3.1999 and all Indian companies which were broadcasters, with a 
minimum 80% Indian share holding and Indian management control were 
permitted to uplink their channels through their own earth station as well. 
The Cabinet in its meeting on 25.7.2000 has decided to further 
liberalise the uplinking policy. As per the new policy, an Indian company, 
which need not be a braodcaster, will be permitted, subject to necessary 
security clearance, to set up uplinking hub or teleport facilities for purposes 
of hiring it out to broadcasters. Permissible foreign equity in such companies 
will be the same as in case of telecom sector, which is persently 49%, 
inclusive of NRI/OCB investments with Indian management control. These 
companies will be permitted to uplink only those TV channels which would 
be specifically approved or permitted by the Government. All TV channels, 
irrespective of their equity holding, ownership or management control will be 
permitted to uplink their programmes from India, subject to necessary 
security clearance, provided they undertake to comply with our broadcasting 
codes. This new policy will not only bring a large number of TV channels 
within the discipline of our broadcasting codes but will also generate 
substantial employment opportunities as India becomes an important hub 
offering state of the art facilities for uplinking. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA) in the Chair] 
Our news agencies have been seriousry handicapped vis-a-vis 
their foreign counterparts as they have been deprived the use of the latest 
technology of Satellite News Gathering (SNG) for purposes of news 
gathering and their further distribution. Because of this handicap, the news 
disseminated by Indian News Agencies reaches the electronic and print 
media late and in the intervening period, contrary point of vie"w remains 
unchallenged in the world media. The new uplinking policy of the 
Government would remove this handicap and permit uplinking facility to the 
Indian News agencies for news gathering and its further distribution to other 
news agencies/broadcasters. For this purpose, Indian news agencies would 
mean those incorporated in India and accredited by the Press 
232 

[26 JULY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Information Bureau and 100% owned by Indians with Indian management 
control. This will give the Indian news agencies the much desired 
competitive edge over the foreign news agencies. 
As in case of earlier policy, such uplinking facilities will be 
permitted with both Indian and foreign satellites. However, proposals 
envisaging Indian satellites will be accorded preferential treatment.

have given notice of a motion for the suspension of the Question Hour and I 
would like to draw your attention to a fact which is very serious. It concerns 
not only the individual Members but also the dignity of the House. Sir, 
yesterday, an item was slated in the List of Business that Mr. Ram Jethmalani 
will make a statement explaining the reasons for his resignation from the 
Council of Ministers. That item was ad mitted, it was listed in the List of 
Business. Thereafter, that item did not come, and when the Chair, after 
transacting the business up to the items preceding that item, took up the next 
item, skipping that particular item, I raised a point of order under rule 23 of 
the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States and 
wanted to know the reasons why that particular item was skipped. Thereafter, 
we were told that the statement which the Member concerned, here Mr. Ram 
Jethmalani, forwarded to the Rajya Sabha Secretariat at 9.45 A.M., was 
running into hundreds of pages and it contained certain contents, certain 
statements, certains facts, certain observations and certain comments which 
cannot be permitted to be told in the House as per the Rules of Procedure and 
Conduct of Business of this House. Therefore, a peculiar situation was created 
and the Chairman satisfied himself that the statement should not be made 
yesterday and we accepted that position because proviso to rule 23 says that if 
the Chairman is satisfied that there arc reasons for deferring a particular item, 
that can be done and we satisfied ourselves. It was expected that the statement 
would come today because 24 hours have passed. But instead of that, there is 
no mention of that particular statement

in the List of Business for today. We do not know as to what has happened. 
But in between in the morning newspapers, we read: "supposed to be the 
statement, alleged to be the statement," Nobody is there to authenticate and it 
is stated there that he did not resign. He was sacked by the Prime Minister. 
Knowing fully well, Mr. Chairman said that this House has no responsibility 
so far as the Confidence Motion or No Confidence Motion on the Council of 
Ministers is concerned. That is the job of the other House. But surely, this 
House has the right to have information as to what actually happened. We 
thought that we are the privileged one, because the Minister who resigned 
belongs to this House. He will come to this House and explain the reasons 
which compelled him to resign from the Council of Minister, and we were 
quite happy when the statement was recorded that he is going to make a 
statement. Now, not only that, we are told, that too through the newspapers 
again—the Member could have come to the House, could have mentioned it, 
could have tried to take his colleagues into confidence—that if the Rajya 
Sabha does not give him time to make a statement by today, then, he should 
have the option to withdraw his offer. Sir, is Rajya Sabha a bargaining 
Council? Can any Member of this House take this House for granted that he 
would like to make a particular statement and can he fix a deadline that if he is 
not allowed to make his statement by that particular deadline, he withdraws 
his offer? Nobody forced him. As per the practice, the Member concerned 
may opt to make a statement; he may not opt to make a statement. But surely, 
he cannot take the House for granted and make an issue that unless by such 
and such time, he is allowed to make a statement, and if this information 
which you are having is correct, that the contents of the statement which he 
tried to make, cannot be allowed as per the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of

allowed as per rules or what part of the statement cannot be allowed? Is it not 
a case of clear manipulation? If somebody tries to open a bargaining counter    
with     the    Government     or    with     somebody    saying

RESOLUTION 
In order to reduce storage and transit losses of foodgrains at farm and 
commercial level, to modernise the system of handling, storage and 
transportation of the foodgrains procured by the Food Corporation of India 
(FCI) and to bring in additionality of resources through private sector 
involvement, the Government has approved a National Policy on Handling. 
Storage and Transportation of Foodgrains, details of which are given 
below:— 
1. Objective of the Policy 
The main objectives of the policy are: 
i. to reduce storage and transit losses at farm level where about 70% of 
the total foodgrain production is retained and consumed and also to 
encourage the farmers to adopt scientific storage methods. 
ii. to modernise the system of handling, storage and transporatation of 
the foodgrains procured by the Food Corporation of India (FCI). 
iii. to harness efforts and resources of public and private sectors, both 
domestic and foreign, to build and operate infrastructure for introduction of 
bulk handling, storage ant transportation of foodgrains in the country. 
2. Policy for house-hold storage 
2 1 Since the house-hold sector retains about 70% of the total production 
and substantial quantities of foodgrains are wasted due- to 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
improper storage at farm level, the major focus is on the improvement of 
storage standards at farm level. Presently, the only scheme targeting this need 
is the Save Grain Campaign, which popularises the use of metallic and non-
metallic storage structures and educates the farmers about the adoption of 
scientific storage methods. The scheme also aims at 
development/improvement of non-metallic traditional storage structures. 
2.2 In order to have a greater success in this area, following initiatives 
have been approved:— 
(i) introduction of a scheme to encourage use of metal bins as well as 
non-metallic storage structures at individual farm level and construction of 
RCC bins at community level with appropriate financial incentives. 
(ii) strengthening of the existing research and training components of the 
Save Grain Campaign Scheme for scientific storage and preservation of 
foodgrains and their propagation among 
farmers. 
3.   Modernisation   and   Upgradation   of  Bulk   Grain   Handling 
Infrastructure 
3.1 In order to reduce storage losses, it is necessary to develop and 
modernise the infrastructure for integrated bulk handling storage and 
transportation in India. The thrust of the policy should be:— 
(i) encouragement of mechanical harvesting, cleaning and drying at farm 
and mandi level. 
(ii) transportation of grains from farm to silos by specially designed 
trucks. 
(iii) construction of a chain of silos at procurement as well as 
distribution points. 
(iv) transportation of grain from silos to railhead and thereafter to pre-
determined destinations by specially designed trucks/rail wagons (with top 
filling and bottom discharge mechanism) dedicated trains. 
(v) declaration of foodgrains storage as infrastructure. 
48 

[27 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
3.2 For storage of foodgrains procured by the FCI, integrated bulk 
handling facilities with silos of large capacity for wheat along with testing 
facilities for quality control would be created at about 20 identified central 
locations in producing and consuming areas as well as a few port towns. 
These facilities, including the infrastructure for bulk transportation to these 
centres, will be created and maintained in the private sector under the overall 
co-ordination of the FCI. The design of special top filling and bottom 
discharge wagons would be decided in consultation with the Ministry of 
Railways. The Ministry of Railways will also be consulted while deciding the 
locations and the circuits where these wagons would ply. FCI will guarantee 
utilisation of these facilities to the extent of 100% for the first ten years and 
75% for the next ten years. From these points, secondary transportation of 
foodgrains would be made in bag form to about 500 godowns in important 
central locations in different States to be owned and maintained by the FCI. 
Further transportation to the consuming centers for retail distribution under 
the Public Distribution System will be carried out by the State Governments. 
3.3 The private sector will be encouraged to build storage capacities in 
which they will store and maintain foodgrains procured by the Government 
agencies,  for which  they will be entitled to 
storage charges. 
3.4 The private sector participation should be sought and 
encouraged for development of infrastructure for the integrated bulk 
handling, storage and transportation through— 
(i) measures such as Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT), Build-Own-
Lease-Transfer (BOLT), Build-Own-Operate (BOO), Lease-Develop-Operate 
(LDO), Joint Ventures etc. 
(ii) generation of funds through public issues by private enterprises 
(iii) automatic approval for Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) upto 100% 
(iv) loans   from   financial    institutions,    NABARD,    external 
commercial borrowings 
49  

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
(v) fiscal incentives as given below: 
(a) 100% deduction in profit for the purpose of Income Tax  for the 
first five years and 30% deduction in profit for the next five years. 
(b) deduction of 40% of the profit derived by financial institutions 
financing such projects, as provided to financial corporations 
engaged, inter-alia, in providing long term finance for agricultural 
development. 
(c) customs duty exemption for items not manufactured in India, on a 
case-to-case basis, subject to a list of such equipment being 
submitted in advance. 
4. Development of Infrastructure Facilities at Ports 
India has been traditionally the importer of foodgrains and, therefore, the 
infrastructure facilities available at the ports are basically meant for unloading 
operations and not for exports. For unloading operations, ship gears are 
normally used. Even the latest machanised facilities at Jawaharlal Nehru Port, 
Navi Mumbai have been designed for import purposes only. There is also lack 
of general cargo berths at the major ports and very limited warehousing 
facilities are available for the storage of foodgrains at ports. For creating the 
proper port facilities for foodgrains meant for export in due course, the 
infrastructure facilities would have to be developed for which following 
actions are required: 
(i) identification of ports to be developed for purposes of export of 
foodgrains. The distribution of foodgrains traffic may spread over to the 
non-traditional ports which have spare capacity like New Mangalore and 
Cochin ports; (ii) development of more general cargo berths at the ports 
through ports' own investment/private participation; (iii) water 
front/berths can be leased to the users who may be encouraged to put up 
their own facilities; and 
50 

[27 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) development of dedicated modern foodgrains handling facilities at 
selected ports. 
5. Role of the Central Government 
The Central Government would: 
(a) facilitate speedy clearance of projects concerning development 
of infrastructure for bulk handling, transportation and storage of 
foodgrains by setting up an Approval Board competent to take final 
decision; 
(b) enter   into    bilateral    agreements   with    other   countries/ 
international agencies for providing technical/financial assistance; 
(c) take necessary legislative / administrative measures for 
removing   impediments   with   regard   to   stock   control   orders/ 
movement control orders framed by various State Governments; 
(d) utilize the services of an existing independent regulatory mechanism 
for fixing/regulating tariff for various operations, such as cleaning, drying, 
storage; transportation, etc.; 
(e) make     available     facilities    of    the    Railways    for    bulk 
transportation; 
(f) promote negotiable Warehouse Receipt System by which 
farmers could hold their grains back from market and meet their 
working capital/short term requirement by borrowing from Banks 
against these receipts; and 
(g) promote research for development of alternate storage 
technologies like Vacuum Process Storage (VPS) technology which 
would ensure longer shelf life of foodgrains and help export of 
foodgrains in vacuum packs. 
6. Role of State Government 
The State Government would help in: 
(a) acquisition of land required for various projects as for public 
purpose; and  
51 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
(b) making   available   other   facilities   such   as   water,   power, road, 
etc.

*77. SHRI V. P. DURAISAMY:

THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): (a) to (c) The "SAARC Vision Beyond the Year 2000" is the title of 
the Report of the SAARC Group of Eminent. Persons-(GEP) established by 
the Ninth SAARC Summit to undertake a comprehensive appraisal of 
SAARC and identify measures to further enhance the effectiveness of the 
Association. The leaders also decided that the Group should develop a long-
range vision and formulate a perspective plan of action including a SAARC 
Agenda for 2000 and Beyond. 
The GEP's recommendations focused on 3 areas: 
I. A time bound plan for regional economic integration, including 
negotiation of a Treaty for a South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) by 
1999, with implementation commencing in 2000 and achievement of a full 
SAFTA in 2008 for SAARC members and 2010 for SAARC LDCs; 
II. Adoption of a Social Charter for SAARC incorporating social welfare 
targets in the areas of population stabilisation, universal primary    
education,    empowerment    of    women,  poverty 
eradication,    human    resource    development,    and    health 
promotion, nutrition and protection of children; 
III. Reform of SAARC institutions. 
In the Economic field, it also envisaged a SAARC Customs Union, with 
harmonisation of external tariffs by 2015, and a SAARC Economic Union, 
with harmonisation of monetary and fiscal policies by 2020. The GEP 
recommended special measures for the Least Developed Countries to enable 
them to adjust to a Free Trade Area. 
Action taken on the GEP Report was as follows: 
SSARC leaders at the 10th SAARC Submit at Colombo held in July 
1998 accepted two of the GEP's main recommendations—(i) achieving 
SAFTA and (ii) the adoption of a SAARC Social Charter. The leaders agreed 
to set up a Committee of Experts with specific terms of reference for drafting 
a comprehensive, treaty regime for 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
creating a free trade area by 2001. 
The other recommendations in the GEP Report were considered by the 
SAARC Standing Committee of Foreign Secretaries and Council of Ministers 
in Nuwara Eliya in March 1999. There was however no consensus on the long 
term goals of a SAARC Customs Union by 2015 and SAARC Economic 
Union by 2020. It was agreed that these issues would be further discussed. 
The First Meeting of the Committee of Experts on SAFTA was held on 
July 15—17, 1999, in Kathmandu at which its Terms of Reference were 
agreed upon. The second meeting is scheduled to be helf in Kathmandu on 
mutually agreed dated. India has conveyed its agreement to participation in 
the meeting. An Intergovernmental Expert Group is also proposed to be set up 
to commence work on the Social Charter. 
Following the military coup in Pakistan a decision was taken after 
mutual consultations among SAARC member States to postpone the 11th 
SAARC Summit scheduled to be held on November, 26—28, 1999 in 
Kathmandu, Nepal. It may be recalled that Pakistan was also suspended from 
the Commonwealth's decisionmaking Councils and this suspension continues. 
However, postponement of the Summit does to impinge on technical and 
functional cooperation, and SAARC meetings continue to be held at the 
technical and official levels. Thus the following meetings, which India has 
participated in, have taken place:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) Indian cotton is 
discounted in international market due to poor quality of ginning, imperfect 
packing, contamination and higher trash contents. 
(b) to (d) In order to improve the yield and the quality of cotton, the 
Government of India has approved the implementation of a Centrally 
Sponsored scheme of Technology Mission on Cotton in January, 2000. The 
Mission consists of four. Mini-Mission. The Mini-Mission-I on research is to 
be dealt by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research for evolving newer 
and better varieties/ technologies suited to different agro-climatic conditions 
of the country for improving the yield and quality of cotton. 
The department of agriculture and Cooperation is responsible for the 
implementation of Mini-Minssion-II for enhancing production through the 
modification of on-going Scheme of Intensive Cotton Development 
Programme. The Intensive Cotton Development Programme envisages to 
enhance production and productivity through various extension/developmental 
activities such as transfer of technologies by field demonstration-farmers 
training, supply of certified seeds of varieties released during last fifteen years, 
use of water saving devices like sprinkler and drip system, establishment of 
seed delinting machines and various activities of pest control including setting 
up of bioagent unit, surveillance, Integrated Pest Management (IPM), 
demonstration-cum-training supply of sprayers/ pheromone trap/bio-agents. 
The Ministry of Textiles is nodal Ministry for implementation of Mini-
Mission-III and Mini-Mission-IV. The Mini-Mission-III is meant for the 
development of marketing infra-structure by undertaking activities like 
construction of marketing yards, auction centres, grading facilities, 
laboratories for testing quality of cotton. The Mini-MissionrlV aims at 
upgradation and modernisation of ginning and pressing factories for the 
production of better quality cotton.

Sri Lanka-India Joint Statement 
(June 12, 2000) 
The Minister of External Affairs of India, Shri Jaswant Singh made an 
official visit to Sri Lanka, at the invitation of the Government of Sri Lanka, 
from 11th to 12th Jane. During his visit the Minister had discussions with 
President Kumaratunga and Foreign Minister, Lakshman Kadirgamar. He also 
met Mr. Ranil Wickremesinghe, the Leader of the Opposition and 
representatives from other political parties. 
At the commencement of discussions, the visiting Minister reiterated the 
continued commitment of the Government of India to the unity, sovereignty 
and territorial integrity of Sri Lanka. He also expressed the good wishes and 
support of the Government of India to the restoration of a lasting peace, which 
would be possible through a political process that produces a settlement, 
which meets the aspirations of all communities. 
The discussions touched upon the present situation and also the broader 
issues related to the further strengthening of the existing close and friendly 
relations that India and Sri Lanka have traditionally enjoyed. 
President Kumaratunga apprised the visiting Minister of current political   
developments   including   the   consultations   between   the 
164 

[27 July 2000] RAJYA   SABHA 
Government and other political parties and the facilitation efforts of Norway. 
President Kumaratunga welcomed India's offer to be of assistance in the 
humanitarian as well as economic sphere to ease any constraints that may be 
currently faced by Sri Lanka. Shri Jaswant Singh added in this regard that 
India would be prepared to extend to. Sri Lanka a credit facility, on terms to 
be mutually worked out between the two Finance Ministers, amounting to 
USS 100 million. The possibilities of Sri Lanka's purchasing wheat, rice and 
sugar on a counter trade basis from India, were also discussed. 
In conclusion both sides noted that the discussions had been productive 
and that they had enabled the reaching of understandings on the measures

576. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA:  Will the Minister of

(b) by when Government propose to bring these legislations in

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) Among the 8 ILO core 
Conventions, India has ratified 4, namely, Convention No. 29 concerning 
Equal Remuneration, Convention No. 105 concerning Abolition of Forced 
Labour and Convention No. 111 concerning Discrimination (Employment and 
Occupation). A Central Legislation is proposed to be enacted fixing a 
minimum age for admission to employment which should facilitate ratification

Convention No. 87 concerning Freedom of Association and Right to Organise 
and No. 98 concerning Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining are, by 
and large, available to all workers in the country. India has not been able to 
ratify these two conventions because of the reasonable restrictions imposed 
on Government servants. The constitutionality and the reasonableness of 
these restrictions have been upheld by the highest courts in India. Therefore, 
at this stage, there is no proposal to ratify these two Conventions. The 
Parliament will be informed as and when the Government propose to ratify an

(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to improve the existing level of 
social security measures including special old age provisions and health care 
schemes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a ) to (c) ILO's World Labour 
Report, 2000 examined the vital role played by social protection in supporting, 
supplementing and replacing market incomes in the event of old age, 
incapacity for work and unemployment. The Report says that but for those 
who work in the rural or urban sectors in developing countries, there is hardly 
any unemployment protection at all. The Report notes that major Asian 
countries like India have social and health insurance schemes covering 
millions of workers and their families, but the vast majority of the population 
in developing countries, including informal sector wage earners and self-
employed persons have no social protection whatsoever and suggests that the 
major focus must be on the extension of the coverage of these workers. 
At present, there are two major social security schemes in India, namely, 
the Employees Provident Fund Scheme and the Employees State Insurance 
Scheme. However, the benefits of these two schemes arc by and large 
confined to the workers of the organised sector. The 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
recently introduced pension scheme under the Employees Provident Fund 
Scheme is also meant-to take care of the retired workers in their old age. 
Besides, many State Governments have introduced old age and destitute 
pension schemes. Social security for the workers in the informal sector is by 
and large confined to some welfare measures. The scope and coverage of 
these welfare schemes will expanded from time to time. However, it is not 
possible, at this stage, with the present stage of economic development to 
provide comprehensive unemployment insurance and benefits to all sections 
of the work force.

States; and 
(d) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION, MINISTER OF STATE OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE   REFORMS   AND   PUBLIC   
GRIEVANCES 
212 

[27 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND 
PENSIONS AND MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. There are 
certain regions in the country which have not been able to benefit adequately 
from the overall growth process. Growth and development are intimately 
related to the level of economic integration of the various parts of the country and 
the linkages that are formed between the backward and the more developed 
regions. For the most part such regions reflect the inadequate integration of the 
local economics in the wider growth process due to resource constraints, fiscal 
barriers, barriers in inter-State commerce, poor provision of social 
infrastructure, in some instances poor governance etc. 
(c) and (d) Balanced regional development has always been an essential 
component of the Indian Development Strategy. Since not all parts of the 
country are equally well endowed to take advantage of growth opportunities 
and since historical inequalities have not been eliminated, planned 
intervention is required. Planning and Development of an area and allocation 
of funds are primarily th e responsibility of concerned State Governments. 
However, Central Government supplements the efforts of the State 
Governments in dealing with the special problems of designated areas 
through the allocation of Central assi stance and special Central assistance. 
Normal Central assistance for the Annual Plans of States is allocated based on 
the Gadgil formula approved by NDC in December, 1991. The formula inter-
alia gives weightage to population and per capita income so as to ensure 
adequate allocation of Central assistance to backward States and overall 
regional balance. Special Central assistance is given for addressing specific 
problems of certain regions e.g. Hill Area Development Programme 
(HADP)/Western Ghats Development Programme (WGDP) and the Border 
Area Development Programme (BADP).

CCEA. So far 40 cases have been referred to these Committees. Out of 10

Disinvestment Policy of The Government 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I am 
going to raise a discussion on the disinvestment policy of the 
Government, which is an issue of great national importance. Now, the 
Vajpayee Government has changed the policy with regard to 
disinvestment, of course, the disinvestment policy was announced and 
started in 1991. But as Mr. Arun Jaitley himself has said now a 
qualitative and quantitative change has taken place with regard to that 
policy. Now, what they are saying is that instead of piecemeal 
disinvestment, unit-wise and sectoral-wise disinvestment is being 
carried on, and to say the truth, in fact, an aggressive disinvestment is 
being carried on. 
In fact, it seems that the real aim is to demolish and dismantle 
the huge edifice of public sector industries and to privatise them. Such 
a step will be against the national interest of our country. The public 
sector was started on the basis of the Industrial Policy Resolution 
adopted in 1966. Immediately after attaining freedom, the question of 
industrialisation, the question of economic development and such other 
issues had to be tackled. Therefore, in a condition when the 
industrialists of our country were not able to invest enough money for 
industrialisation or budding up the infrastructure, it was felt that the 
Government would have to enter the field in a big way. Thus, these 
public institutions were started, in the past several decades a massive 
investment, nearly Rs. 2.00,000 crores, has been made in the public 
sector. It is a very huge amount. A very big public sector edifice has 
been built up.  Those industries are engaged in producing

called and consulted; our views are being recognised 'and our

Disinvestment Commission, was constituted. By 1999, its term lapsed

what will happen is that the. public sector, which has been built up with

time, in the private sector, more employment opportunities will not be

of small-scale industries are being closed. Now, with the lifting of the

unemployment wilt increase. The same thing is happening in other 
cases 
where prices of other commodities are also going down. Therefore, all

measures will nave to be taken to  find a solution to this problem.

disinvestment, but 
the question of new economic reforms — whether we calf it the second 
stage of reforms or whatever — will have to be reviewed, taking into 
consideration the real situation that is obtaining in the 
country and a solution found. That is what I have to say. Regarding the 
public sector, I would appeal to the Government, through the hon. 
Chairman 
that this attempt at disinvestment should be stopped for the time being, 
the 
matter should be seriously considered and a public debate should take

*83. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted any survey of the working of the 
Mid-day Meal Scheme for school children launched by Government in 1995; 
(b) if so, what are the findings of this survey report; and 
(c) what measures are being taken to plug the loopholes and deficiencies in 
implementation of the scheme as, revealed by the survey report? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) An evaluation has been undertaken in 10 States to assess the efficiency 
and effectiveness of the National Programme for Nutritional Support to Primary 
Education (Mid-Day Meals Scheme) by an independent agency, Operation Research 
Group, New Delhi. The study covers Assam, Gujarat, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, 
Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa,'Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The 
report was submitted in September, 1999. The findings of the report state that while 
the programme has given boost to enrolm ent in Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar 
Pradesh and West Bengal; in 6 other States  it has had positive impact on attendance 
and retention. 
Besides, a study conducted by NCERT on States policies on Incentive Schemes in 
Primary Schools and their Contribution to Girls' Participation, completed in April, 
2000, also covers the Mid-day Meal Scheme in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. The 
report states that the Noon Meal Scheme of Tamil Nadu and supply of food-grains 
under MDM in Uttar Pradesh have helped improve the enrolment and retention of girls 
in schools.

time, the Government has taken steps to improve the monitoring and supervision of the 
programme at all levels, create a greater awareness regarding the programme through 
involvement of Village Education Committees, streamline procedures so as to ensure 
regular supply of food-grains and timely reimbursement of transportation charges and 
payment to Food Corporation of India and ensure a more rigorous role for the nodal 
agency for programme implementation at the State level.

(a) to (d) One normal coloured Tiger died in Nandankanan Zoo on 23rd June, 
2000. The postmortem reports confirme d that the animal died because of 
Trypanosomiasis, Another tiger showed symptoms of same sickness on 2nd July, 
2000. Therefore, the zoo authorities administ ered 'Berenil to 16 tigers of adjoining 
enclosures, after taking them into a squeezed cage. The animal which showed sign of 
sickness on 2nd July died on 4th July. Of the remaining 15 tigers which were 
administered drug on 3rd July, 8 tigers (six white and two coloured) died between 4th 
and 5th July, 2000. One white tiger each died on 6th and 7th July, 2000 respectively, ft 
has also been revealed that 5 tigers got infection of the same disease in 1999 of which 
3 died. One of the survivors of 1999 was amongst the 12 tigers died between 23rd June 
to 7th July 2000. 
The Central Government was informed of the deaths on the morning of 5th July, 
2000. The Ministry appointed an Expert Committee to find out the causes of death and 
to suggest ways and means to prevent recurrence of such happenings on 6th July, 
2000. The Committee was asked to start its work from 7th July and to give their report 
by 15th July, 2000. In the interim period the Ministry also decided to have an expert 
consultation to discuss the events at Nandankanan Zoo on 19th and 20th July, 2000.

The Ministry is of the definite view that the response of zoo administration was

measures after the death of 3 tigers during 1999 from the same disease and again after

treatment to the animals between 23rd June to 2nd July, 2000. These views have been 
communicated to the State Govt, to take necessary disciplinary action against the 
persons responsible for the lapse.

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): 
(a) to (d) India was among the first countries globally to launch a- National Family Welfare 
Programme, in 1952, with the objective of reducing birth rates to the extent necessary to 
stabilize the population at a level consistent with the requirement of national economy. In 
keeping with the democratic tradition of( the country, the family welfare programme seeks to: 
(w) promote responsible and planned parenthood through voluntary and informed choice 
of family planning methods best suited to individual acceptors, and 
(x) continue the target free approach in administering family planning services. 
We do not perceive that India needs compulsory sterilization. Our past experience indicates 
that it neither feasible nor desirable to put in place harsh or coercive measures for the 
promotion of compulsory sterilization. During 1970s, Family Welfare Programme focused 
primarily on terminal methods and received a setback on account of the rigid target based 
approach and coercion adopted during implementation. The Family Welfare Programme is 
today fully voluntary, target free and as well as need based. Our emphasis is on providing 
wider coverage and outreach of services

while   encouraging   citizens   through   information,   education   and communication to access 
the services and facilities provided. 
In particular remarkable progress has been made in the area of population stabilization in 
Kerala, Goa and Tamil Nadu without any coercion or compulsion. There is no proposal to make 
sterilization compulsory. 
The Government is extremely concerned about, improving the quality of life of its citizens 
by making reproductive health care accessible and affordable to all. besides also increasing the 
provision and outreach of primary and secondary education, extending basic amenities 
including sanitation, safe drinking water and housing, besides empowering women and 
enhancing their employment opportunities, and providing transport and communication. 
Accordingly, Government has recently taken the following steps: 
 1997 — Launched the Reproductive and Child Health Programme which has put in 
place the target free approach in the administration of Family Planning services. 
 February 2000 •— Adopted the National Population Policy 2000 which seeks to put in 
place an inter-sectoral agenda for achieving the goals and objectives of population 
stabilization. 
A large number of factors influence population growth rated and in turn are affected by it. 
Some of these factors are women's empowerment, women's status in the family, education 
particularly of women, and some other factors. Our actual success in containing the growth of 
population is dependent on: 
(i) Publicly stated support by the national level, state level and community level leaders; 
(ii) Efficiency and accountability within the State Health Systems for ensuring effective 
delivery of services to citizens; 
(iii) Women's education and women's status in the family; 
(iv) Resources assigned for population related programmes. 
Government has adopted a National Population Policy in February, 2000 which provides

million liters per day. With the commissioning of 9 out of 16 sewage treatment plants under 
construction, about 14-00 million litres per day of sewage is treated and the remaining 1320 
million litres per day is discharged untreated into Yamuna river. Due to delay in completion of

Plan was approved by the Government in April 1993. The present approved cost of the Action 
Plan is Rs.509.45. crore. Under this Plan, works have been taken in 21 towns out of which 8

unauthorized colonies and slums. The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi have 
also decided to undertake complete rehabilitation of the sewerage system so that all the surface 
drains presently discharging waste water into the river are intercepted and diverted for

RAMACHANDRAIAH RUMANDLA: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether 700 million gallons of raw sewa ge flows into the Yamuna river every 
day, affecting health of 12 million people; and 
 if so, the action taken by the Central Pollution Control Board to get the Yamuna 
river in md around Delhi cleaned, get rid of sewage discharge and to instal treatment 
plant to tackle such enormous waste? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI):    (a)   According   to   a   study   
conducted   by   the 
88 

[28 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Water and Power Consultancy Services (In^ia) Limited in April 1999, the quantity of 
sewage generated in Delhi was estimated at 600 million gallons per day. With the 
commissioning of 9 out of 16 sewage treatment plants under construction, about 300 
million gallons per day of sewage is treated and the remaining 300 million gallons per 
day is discharged untreated into Yamuna river. In addition, due to delay in completion 
of the 15 common effluent treatment plants in 21 industrial estates of Delhi, industrial 
effluents are discharged untreated into the river. As a result, the Yamuna river has been 
rendered unfit for bathing. 
(b) Following steps have been taken by  the Government of National Capital 
Territory of Delhi to minimize the pollution of river Yamuna: 
(i) Water polluting industries have been directed vide public notice in the 
newspapers to stop discharging untreated industrial effluents directly or 
indirectly into river Yamuna with effect from 1-11-99. 
(ii) A total of 3177 water polluting industries have been closed as on 6-7-2000. 
(iii) A total of 1121 units have installed effluent treatment plants. 
(iv) 550 water polluting units in non conforming areas have been allotted industrial 
plots in Narela Industrial complex. 
(v) 8 Project Directors have been appointed for 8 major drains to supervise the work 
of identification of water polluting units and also cleaning operation of the 
drains, 
(vi) 9 sewage treatment plants have be en put into use out of 16 new sewage 
treatment plants. Of the remaining 7 treatment plants, 6 will be completed by 
March, 2001 and tenders for the remaining one sewage treatment plant have 
been invited. 
(vii) The quantity of sewage undergoing treatment has been increased from about 
1000 million litres per day to 1400 million litres per day. By December 2000, 
about 1730 million litres per day of sewage would be treated and by March 
2001, this would increase to 1840 million litres per day.

Curbing emission of green house gases 
660. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will th e Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 what effective steps have been taken so far by Government to crub emission of 
green house gases, since signing of the convention to crub emission of such gases; and 
 whether Government agree with the US-President's reported speech at a 
Democratic Leadership Council.in Washington on may 21-22, 2000 that India and 
China were expected to become bigger em itters of green house gases than US in 
another 30 years, and if not, the steps contemplated to avert the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) Several existing 'policy declarations', 
'acts as well as various fiscal and on-going  programmes/initiatives contribute to the 
minimization of greenhouse gas emissions in India. Such measures include 
improvement of the efficiency of c onventional energy generation and use, 
development of major renewable energy programmes 'promotion, of clean coal and 
bio-mass energy technologies as well as conservation of forests. 
(b) The existing legal and policy framework adequately addresses the concerns of 
greenhouse gas emissions. The Convention recognizes that per-capita emissions in 
developing countries are still relatively low and that the share of emissions originating 
a developing countries will grow to meet their social and development needs. Thus, in 
the context of multilateral obligations, India is not required to take any steps to 'curb 
the green house gas emissions' and/or 'avert the situation' arising out .of their possible 
build-up in the atmosphere.

 what is the ex of pollution of river Yamuna at the point of entry and exit it from NCT

 What are the reasons for pollution of the river; and

pollution? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS 
(SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) According to the monitoring report for the months of May 
and June, 2000 of the Central Pollution Control Board, the bio-chemical oxygen demand and 
the dissolved oxygen-the two indicators of the health' of a water body-in the river water at the 
entry point to Delhi are 2 milligram per liter and 7 milligram per liter respectively. At the Okhla 
barrage which & the exist point of the river from Delhi, the values of the bio-chemical oxygen 
and the dissolved oxygen are 35 milligram per liter and 'nil' respectively. The prescribed 
standards for these values for the river Yamuna are 3 milligram per liter and 5 milligram per 
liter respectively. The report indicates that the river Yamuna gets significantly polluted in its 
stretch along Delhi due to discharge of municipal sewage and industrial effluents in partly 
treated and mostly untreated conditions. 
 discharge of municipal sewage and industrial effluents in partly treated and partly 
untreated conditions is the main reason of pollution of river Yamuna along Delhi. 
 Following steps have been taken by the Government of National Capital Territory of 
Delhi to minimize the pollution of river Yamuna:— 
(i) Water polluting industries have been directed vide public notice in the newspapers to stop 
discharging untreated industrial effluents direct!\ or indirectly into river Yamuna with

 whether it was mentioned at the WHO Conference in Amsterdam that 30 lakhs

TB and India accounts for about 30% of TB patients in the world. 
(c) The National TB Control programme has been accorded high priority in India 
and is included under the 20-Point Programme. The main thrust is on early detection of 
the infectious sputum positive TB cases aid on treating them effectively. 
The Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) which aims at curing 85% 
of the new sputum positive cases and to detect at
